A new statue has today been unveiled to commemorate the life and work of biologist, Dr Charles Darvi. Darvi was the head researcher that led an expedition to the Chagos Islands in 2027, revealing new information about the birds and other wildlife on the islands including revelations about the dodo. The research project was tragically cut short with the news of Darvi's death in early September 2028.

Darvi was returning to the Mauritius mainland, when a freak storm hit. His boat was hit with high speed winds, notoriously bad at that time of year on the east coast. This caused it to capsize, dragging its fourteen crew members down with it. Fortunately, a crew of Mauritian coastguard were patrolling close by and were able to recover thirteen of the crew. However, the doctor was not found with the rest of his research team. A search party was launched in hopes of finding the biologist, however no trace of him could be found. Dr Charles Darvi was then pronounced legally deceased after 6 months of fruitless search.

This news shocked the nation and the field of Biology as a whole. Plans were put in place last year to commission a statue of Darvi to be erected at Port Louis university. Kumar Singh then designed and then created a life size, bronze statue to be placed in the university atrium. Praying Jugnauth and Darvi's former colleagues were present at the unveiling. Two members of the research project flew in from their honeymoon to be there to pay their respects to Charles. Hans and Anna Muller were both good friends of Darvi's and were married two weeks ago.

Anna was one of several speakers who made speeches at the unveiling. She had this to say:

'Charles was not only a brilliant scientist, but a fantastic friend. I regret every minute that I didn't speak to you. My life will never be the same without you, Charles. I miss you so much. I love you'.

At this point Mrs Muller broke down in tears and was comforted by her husband. The event finished with a speech from Pravind Jugnauth, announcing that the biology department at the university was to be renamed the 'Charles Darvi Institute of Biology'.
